      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "Is 72 DPI the same as web resolution?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "No, and this is one I get asked about constantly. 72 DPI is a legacy tag left over from early Macintosh displays and it doesn't describe modern web resolution at all. From my experience preparing images for social media, what actually matters on the web is the pixel dimensions of the image, not the DPI value stored in its metadata. I can confirm from testing: a 1000 by 1000 pixel image displays identically at 72 DPI or 300 DPI in any browser, because the browser only reads the pixel count."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "Why is 300 DPI the standard for print?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "I've always found it interesting that 300 DPI became the print standard for a very human reason: it exceeds the resolving power of the human eye at typical reading distances of 25 to 30 centimeters. Below 300 DPI, I can sometimes spot individual dots on close inspection, especially in fine detail and small text. Above 300 DPI, the improvement is imperceptible to me and most viewers, so 300 became the widely accepted sweet spot between quality and file size."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "Can I change the DPI of an image to make it print better?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "I wish I could say yes, but changing the DPI tag alone does not improve print quality. I learned this the hard way early on. Print sharpness is determined by the total pixel count divided by the physical print size. A 600 by 600 pixel image tagged as 300 DPI will still print at only 2 by 2 inches, no matter what number I put in the metadata. To print larger without softness, the image needs more actual pixels, which requires either a higher-resolution source or careful upscaling."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "Does DPI matter for Instagram or other social media?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "Not at all. I post to Instagram, Facebook, and X regularly, and I can tell you that DPI does not matter for any of them. Every social platform I've tested displays images on screens, which are pixel-based devices. The platforms read only the pixel dimensions of an upload and ignore the DPI metadata entirely. What I focus on — and what I'd recommend — is getting the correct pixel dimensions for each platform."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "What resolution do I need for a large poster print?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "It depends on how far away people will stand from it. When I print a 24 by 36 inch poster that'll be viewed up close, I aim for roughly 7200 by 10800 pixels at 300 DPI. But for a poster meant to hang on a wall where people view it from several feet away, I've successfully dropped to 150 DPI — about 3600 by 5400 pixels — without any visible loss of quality. Most print shops I've worked with accept 150 to 200 DPI for large-format work because the eye simply can't resolve finer detail at typical viewing distances."
        }
      }
